subject: Computer Networking
title: Phishing Attacks
description: A short lesson to help you apply Phishing Attacks.

hook.text: An email from your bank says 'Verify your account now.' The link looks right. But the site is fake.

buildup.text: Phishing uses fake emails, sites, or messages to trick you into entering credentials or downloading malware.

discovery.text: Spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalized details. It's far more convincing than mass campaigns.

twist.text: AI now generates phishing emails without grammar mistakes. The old 'look for typos' advice no longer works.

climax.text: Hardware security keys and passkeys eliminate phishing risk for login. The key only works on the real site.

punchline.text: Phishing doesn't hack systems. It hacks trust.

quiz.question: What makes spear phishing more dangerous than regular phishing?
options: It targets specific individuals with personalized details
It only works on mobile devices

details.summary: Phishing attacks use deceptive emails, messages, or websites that impersonate trusted entities to trick users into revealing credentials, clicking malicious links, or downloading malware.
details.whyItMatters: Phishing is the most common initial attack vector for data breaches. Technical defenses alone cannot stop it — user awareness combined with email security layers are both essential.
takeaways: Phishing impersonates trusted entities to steal credentials
Spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalized lures
Multi-layered defenses combine email filtering with user training

faq.question: How can you identify a phishing email?
faq.answer: Check the sender's actual email address, not just the display name. Look for urgency or threatening language. Hover over links to verify the URL before clicking. Watch for grammatical errors and generic greetings. Legitimate organizations rarely ask for passwords or sensitive data via email.

faq.question: What is spear phishing?
faq.answer: Spear phishing targets specific individuals using information gathered from social media, company websites, and data breaches. A spear phishing email might reference a real project, use a colleague's name, or mimic an expected invoice.
